Task 24 on branch `cleaning` (this worktree). Design only: write two docs, no code. Do not run `next start` or `next dev`. Do not read or print secret values; never create .env files. Never run `npm run build:book` (paid APIs). Never touch data/books/oz. Read `.agents/skills/architect/SKILL.md` and `.agents/skills/unslop/SKILL.md` and follow them (they are user-invocable only, so read the files instead of invoking them). Proceed without asking questions. ## Goal (owner) A cleaning layer before segmentation that removes everything that is not the book itself: publisher info, copyright and title pages, tables of contents, license text, ads for other books, transcriber notes, colophons, "about the author". A deterministic pass first (EPUB semantics, spine, known patterns), then one fast cheap LLM call that classifies only the ambiguous sections and the boundary blocks. Output: cleaned chapters plus a dev-visible report of what was removed and why. One shared entry point for Library books and user uploads: EPUB first, the current Gutenberg .txt path stays as fallback. Oz must not change: `data/books/oz/book.json` textVersion `sha256:00c257db…` stays as is (Oz keeps the txt path). ## Write 1. `docs/research/cleaning.md`: concise findings from the samples below (what each source looks like, what junk appears where, what is reliable and what is not). Under 120 lines. 2. `docs/tasks/24-cleaning.md`: the design (types, rules in order, LLM call, report shape, entry points, tests, what is out of scope). Under 220 lines. Make concrete decisions; the implementer follows it literally. ## Findings (researched by hand; trimmed fixtures are in core/fixtures/clean/) Samples: Gutenberg EPUB3 pg55 (Oz), pg11 (Alice), pg54 (Marvelous Land of Oz, 27 MB with images, EPUB2 no-images build 228 KB), pg63361 (Cottage Folk, Heinemann 1897), pg77472 (Pan's Garden, Macmillan 1912); Standard Ebooks Oz and A Christmas Carol. Fixture shape (one JSON per book): `{meta:{title}, sections:[{id, href, linear, types, docTitle, navLabel, words, blocks:[{text, heading}]}]}`. `types` = epub:type tokens on body and its top-level section. `blocks` = leaf block elements (p, div, li, blockquote, h1-h6, td, dt, dd, pre, figcaption without block children) with whitespace collapsed and `
` as a single space; elements whose id starts with `pg-` or equals `project-gutenberg-license` already removed. Fixtures keep only a few blocks per section (first/last ones, short lines, a window around "THE END"); `words` is the untrimmed count. Gutenberg EPUB (all PG samples): - No epub:type, no landmarks, guide empty. Spine: `wrap0000.xhtml` cover (svg only), then `_-h-N.htm.xhtml`. - h-0 holds the PG header (`#pg-header-heading`, `#pg-machine-header`, `#pg-start-separator`), title page and often the Contents table. Last file holds `#pg-end-separator`, `#project-gutenberg-license`, `#pg-footer-heading` (about 2,900 words). With pg- ids removed both are near empty. - Each file's `` repeats the chapter heading. Heading blocks: Oz h-2 starts with heading "The Wonderful Wizard of Oz" (book title) then "Chapter I The Cyclone"; chapter files use `Chapter II<br/>The Council with the Munchkins`. Oz h-1 is the Introduction (185 words), which the current txt ingest drops. Chapter XXIV is a real 80-word chapter. - Checked: Oz EPUB body blocks from h-2..h-25 (non-heading, minus `[Illustration…]`) equal the 1104 txt paragraphs in book.json exactly (with `<br>` as space; `<br>` as newline differs on one verse paragraph). - Alice: "CHAPTER I. Down the Rabbit-Hole" headings, ends with block "THE END". Land of Oz: headings have no "Chapter" word ("Tip Manufactures a Pumpkinhead"); h-0 has the author's note + contents. - Cottage Folk: h-0 = transcriber's note + ads for another novel ("In One Volume, Crown 8vo, price 6s.", press quotes "The Spectator.—“…") + title page ("London / William Heinemann / 1897 / All rights reserved"). h-1 CONTENTS with page numbers. Stories h-2..h-9 have uppercase titles (no chapter word). Ads start inside h-9, after "THE END" and the printer line "Richard Clay & Sons, Limited, London & Bungay.", about 200 blocks of book titles, "In One Volume, price 6s." and press quotes. h-10 = more ads + transcriber corrections table ("206.15", "Added."). - Pan's Garden: h-1 Macmillan imprint cities, h-2 half-title, h-3 title page, h-4 copyright + dedication, h-5 PREFATORY NOTE, h-6 CONTENTS. Tiny continuation files with no heading (h-8 "Holmesly.", h-17 "Helouan.", h-24 "Sussex." + "Printed by R. & R. Clark, Limited, Edinburgh.") are the sign-off of the previous story; their `<title>` equals the previous story's. h-25..31 are "By ALGERNON BLACKWOOD" ads ("Crown 8vo. 6s.", "net", "MACMILLAN AND CO., Ltd., LONDON"), h-32 TRANSCRIBER'S NOTE, h-33 license. - Keyword matching alone is unsafe: The Railway Children (pg1874) has an in-story "advertisement" game. Standard Ebooks: full semantics. Sections typed `frontmatter titlepage`, `frontmatter imprint`, `frontmatter introduction|preface z3998:non-fiction`, `frontmatter halftitlepage`, `bodymatter chapter z3998:fiction`, `backmatter colophon`, `backmatter copyright-page`. Chapter headings are just "I" / "Stave I"; the nav label carries the title ("I: The Cyclone", "Stave I: Marley’s Ghost"). Text differs from Gutenberg (modernized edition), so SE Oz is not a drop-in source for Oz. Existing code to reuse: `core/gutenberg.ts` (stripGutenberg, splitChapters, buildBook, canonicalLines), `pipeline/ingest.ts` (runIngest, textVersion drift check), `pipeline/meta.ts` (createMetaClient: json_schema strict, returns token usage), `pipeline/prices.ts` (metaCostUsd). A home page branch (task 20, not merged yet) adds `core/epub.ts`: a client-safe parser with fflate 0.8.3 `unzipSync` + platform DOMParser, MAX_EPUB_BYTES 20 MB, EpubError codes, a zip-bomb guard (8 MB per entry, 60 MB inflated), DRM detection, OPF/nav/NCX parsing, but it returns only title, author, chapter titles, word count and cover. Design the EPUB section reader so it can live in that file once it lands (same deps, same guards); until then a new `core/epub-sections.ts` with the DOM parser injected as an argument (jsdom 30.1.3 devDep in Node, DOMParser in the browser). ## Design direction (decide details, keep the spirit) - `core/clean.ts` is pure (AGENTS.md: no env, no network). Input: book title + RawSection[] (fixture shape minus `words`). The LLM is injected as a `judge` function; tests use fakes. - Deterministic rules, in order, each removal recorded with rule id and reason: linear="no"; epub:type frontmatter/backmatter (and the specific types) removed, bodymatter/chapter kept as confident content; empty or heading-only sections; PG license/markers; title patterns (contents, transcriber's note, advertisements, colophon, copyright, index, also by, about the author, preface/introduction/foreword/prefatory note: removed by policy, matches today's Oz); contents-like bodies (short lines with page numbers); ad-like bodies (prices "6s.", "net", "Crown 8vo", "In One Volume", press quotes, publisher address lines) above a share threshold; continuation merge (no heading, few words, same docTitle as the previous kept section); chapter-heading regex = confident content. Inside content: drop heading blocks from paragraphs (they make the title), drop `[Illustration…]`, cut after the last "THE END"/"FINIS" in the last content section, drop trailing printer lines. - Everything not decided goes to ONE LLM call per book: each ambiguous section as id + title guess + word count + first/last blocks (truncated), plus the first blocks of the first content section and the last blocks of the last one with indexes. Strict JSON: per-section verdict content | non_content | uncertain with a kind and a short reason; head and tail cut counts. Safety: uncertain and missing ids are kept and flagged; never drop a long interior section on the LLM's word alone (keep + flag); clamp cuts; on LLM failure keep the deterministic result and record `llm: failed` (no raw error). Book text is untrusted data in the prompt (prompt injection from uploads). - Title derivation: first heading block that is not the book title, minus a leading label (Chapter/Stave/Book/Part + numeral, or bare numeral); if only a label remains use the nav label's text after ":". - Report: source, kept chapters (title, paragraph count, section ids), removed (section or block range, kind, reason, rule or llm, words, short preview), flagged, merged, llm usage (model, tokens, costUsd) or null. - Entry points: `cleanSections` (core), an EPUB section reader (core, client-safe), the Gutenberg txt path wrapped to return the same {chapters, report} shape with zero LLM calls and exactly today's splitChapters output, `pipeline/ingest.ts` choosing EPUB when the book config says so (Oz stays txt), and a dev CLI `npm run clean:epub -- <file.epub> [--no-llm]` that prints a summary and writes the full report JSON to `pipeline/out/clean/` (gitignore it). - LLM: Muse Spark via META_API_KEY with `createMetaClient`, model `CLEAN_MODEL ?? "muse-spark-1.3-contributor"`. No Baseten key exists; note that Baseten Model APIs are OpenAI-compatible (`https://inference.baseten.co/v1`, Bearer BASETEN_API_KEY), so a Llama 4 Scout judge is a base URL + model swap later. Do not build it. - User uploads: the browser can run the deterministic pass; the LLM pass needs a server route with spend guards, which is out of scope here. Commit both docs: "Add cleaning research note and task 24 design".

event.chunk:
Read text file `.agents/skills/unslop/SKILL.md`.
1|---
2|name: unslop
3|description: Cut AI tells from any writing.
4|disable-model-invocation: true
5|---
6|
7|# Unslop
8|
9|Edit text to remove AI patterns. Scan for the patterns below, then rewrite. Preserve meaning and match the intended tone.
10|
11|## Patterns to detect and fix
12|
13|Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite. A removed rule leaves a gap.
14|
15|### Content
16|
17|3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
18|5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.
19|
20|### Language
21|
22|7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
23|8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Say "is" or "has".
24|9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
25|10. **Rule of three.** Don't force ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
26|11. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
27|12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.
28|
29|### Style
30|
31|13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
32|14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example, not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
33|15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
34|16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell.
35|17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
36|18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
37|19. **Curly quotes.** Use straight quotes.
38|
39|### Communication artifacts
40|
41|20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
42|22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.
43|
44|### Filler
45|
46|23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". Delete "It is important to note that".
47|24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
48|25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.
49|
50|### Jargon
51|
52|26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate (base), wedge, wedge in (add), vector (way, method), locus, vantage, nexus, primitive as a noun, harness as a metaphor, surface as in "API surface", bedrock, scaffolding as a metaphor, modality, paradigm, gold-plating (more than the job needs), ratchet as a metaphor (the mechanism's real name, or a limit that only tightens), evacuate for moving code (move out), endgame (the last phase), north star, flywheel. These read as technical but usually have a plainer concrete word. Pick the concrete word.
53|
54|### Plain speech
55|
56|27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". Ask what the sentence tells the reader to do or know, then write that. If you can't restate it as a concrete instruction, fact, or number, cut it. One more check: if the sentence could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
57|28. **Shorten or split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop clauses. One idea per sentence.
58|29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Catch "is/are/was/were + past participle" and name the actor: "queries are validated" becomes "the compiler validates queries", "the file is parsed by the loader" becomes "the loader parses the file". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.
59|30. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number, and "significantly improves" becomes the measured delta. An adverb propping up a weak verb means the verb is wrong.
60|31. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" and "leverage" become "use", "facilitate" becomes "help", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if". The fancier synonym is rarely clearer.
61|32. **Mannered prose.** Metaphor or flourish where a literal phrase exists: aphorisms ("wire it or delete it"), rhetorical fragments for effect, personified code ("the plan holds it"), figurative verbs ("rides along", "stands on"), stock framing phrases. "A dial worth turning" becomes "a parameter worth varying". Say what you mean. Rule 26 covers the metaphor nouns.
62|33. **Over-compression.** Dropped articles, verbless fragments, symbol-speak, and abbreviations that make the reader decode instead of read. "Parser rejects bad date → exit 2, no write" becomes "The parser rejects a bad date, exits with code 2, and writes nothing." Write whole sentences with their articles and verbs, and spell out arrows and abbreviations.

Read text file `.agents/skills/architect/SKILL.md`.
1|---
2|name: architect
3|description: "Sketch types, signatures, and module structure before code, then stay in the loop while implementation fills in. Use for /architect, 'architect this', 'design this', or non-trivial work where jumping to code would lock in the wrong shape."
4|disable-model-invocation: true
5|---
6|
7|# Architect
8|
9|Sketch types, function signatures, class shapes, and module boundaries with `not implemented` bodies and pseudocode. Synthesize across multiple model perspectives, then fill in code against the chosen sketch.
10|
11|## Start
12|
13|Open a todolist with one entry per phase before starting.
14|
15|1. Ground
16|2. Sketch
17|3. Agree
18|4. Implement
19|5. Scrap
20|
21|## Phase A: Ground the problem
22|
23|Build a real mental model of every system the new code touches. Run the **how** skill over the relevant subsystems. Naming a file isn't grounding. Produce the architectural explanation `how` prescribes. If the design redefines ownership or layering, also run the **why** skill on the existing shape so the rationale becomes a constraint, not a guess.
24|
25|Skip Phase A only when the work is genuinely greenfield with no surrounding system to integrate.
26|
27|## Phase B: Sketch
28|
29|Run the **arena** skill with the design-sketch task and the Phase A grounding artifacts. Pass `references/runner-prompt.md` as each runner's prompt.
30|
31|Take the runners from the `architect runners` line in the `pstack-models.mdc` rule, in place of the `arena runners` line. If the rule or that line is missing, use `claude-opus-5-5-xhigh` and `grok-4.7-xhigh-fast`. Alias and rejected entries follow the runner rules in the **arena** skill's Phase A.
32|
33|Design it twice. Require at least two structurally distinct candidates before synthesis, even when the first looks sufficient. This is the **exhaust-the-design-space** principle skill made concrete. Whole-shape alternatives, not point fixes inside one shape.
34|
35|Screen every candidate against [`references/design-red-flags.md`](references/design-red-flags.md) before synthesis. Assume the next contributor is an agent that sees only the files it opened, copies the nearest example, and takes the shortest path that compiles. Prefer the design where a change that looks right from one file is right for the whole repo.
36|
37|Compare viable candidates on interface depth. Prefer the design that hides more complexity behind a smaller, simpler public surface. A rich interface can keep call chains short by concentrating capability instead of scattering it across layers.
38|
39|Arena returns one synthesized design package. Its synthesis decision fills the rationale's "Synthesis decision" section.
40|
41|## Phase C: Agree (opt-in)
42|
43|Default: proceed directly to implementation with the synthesized design. No human checkpoint.
44|
45|Opt in to a checkpoint when the invoker explicitly asks: "/architect with checkpoint," "stop and show me before implementing," or similar. Then surface the synthesized design and pause for sign-off.
46|
47|The synthesis can ship as its own commit either way, as the "scaffold first" mode of the **foundational-thinking** principle skill. Planned and scoped breakage during fill-in is fine, per the **outcome-oriented-execution** principle skill. For adversarial pressure on the design before implementing, run the **interrogate** skill on the synthesized sketch.
48|
49|If the human pushes back on the shape (in a checkpoint or after the fact), treat that as Phase A evidence. Re-ground and re-run Phase B before writing more code.
50|
51|## Phase D: Implement against the sketch
52|
53|Replace `not implemented` bodies with code, pseudocode with logic. The synthesized sketch is the contract. Deviations from it are signal to surface, not friction to absorb silently. 1|---
2|name: unslop
3|description: Cut AI tells from any writing.
4|disable-model-invocation: true
5|---
6|
7|# Unslop
8|
9|Edit text to remove AI patterns. Scan for the patterns below, then rewrite. Preserve meaning and match the intended tone.
10|
11|## Patterns to detect and fix
12|
13|Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite. A removed rule leaves a gap.
14|
15|### Content
16|
17|3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
18|5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.
19|
20|### Language
21|
22|7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
23|8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Say "is" or "has".
24|9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
25|10. **Rule of three.** Don't force ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
26|11. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
27|12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.
28|
29|### Style
30|
31|13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
32|14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example, not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
33|15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
34|16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell.
35|17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
36|18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
37|19. **Curly quotes.** Use straight quotes.
38|
39|### Communication artifacts
40|
41|20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
42|22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.
43|
44|### Filler
45|
46|23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". Delete "It is important to note that".
47|24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
48|25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.
49|
50|### Jargon
51|
52|26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate (base), wedge, wedge in (add), vector (way, method), locus, vantage, nexus, primitive as a noun, harness as a metaphor, surface as in "API surface", bedrock, scaffolding as a metaphor, modality, paradigm, gold-plating (more than the job needs), ratchet as a metaphor (the mechanism's real name, or a limit that only tightens), evacuate for moving code (move out), endgame (the last phase), north star, flywheel. These read as technical but usually have a plainer concrete word. Pick the concrete word.
53|
54|### Plain speech
55|
56|27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". Ask what the sentence tells the reader to do or know, then write that. If you can't restate it as a concrete instruction, fact, or number, cut it. One more check: if the sentence could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
57|28. **Shorten or split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop clauses. One idea per sentence.
58|29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Catch "is/are/was/were + past participle" and name the actor: "queries are validated" becomes "the compiler validates queries", "the file is parsed by the loader" becomes "the loader parses the file". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.
59|30. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number, and "significantly improves" becomes the measured delta. An adverb propping up a weak verb means the verb is wrong.
60|31. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" and "leverage" become "use", "facilitate" becomes "help", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if". The fancier synonym is rarely clearer.
61|32. **Mannered prose.** Metaphor or flourish where a literal phrase exists: aphorisms ("wire it or delete it"), rhetorical fragments for effect, personified code ("the plan holds it"), figurative verbs ("rides along", "stands on"), stock framing phrases. "A dial worth turning" becomes "a parameter worth varying". Say what you mean. Rule 26 covers the metaphor nouns.
62|33. **Over-compression.** Dropped articles, verbless fragments, symbol-speak, and abbreviations that make the reader decode instead of read. "Parser rejects bad date → exit 2, no write" becomes "The parser rejects a bad date, exits with code 2, and writes nothing." Write whole sentences with their articles and verbs, and spell out arrows and abbreviations.

# Git source-control safety

The working tree belongs to the user. Make the change, leave it visible, and
let them decide what becomes history.

## Never without an explicit ask

The user must have asked for that exact write in this session, in their own
words. An explicit request to create a new commit counts anywhere in the user's
own task text, but it is not a request to amend, push, or tag. Finishing a task
without that request does not authorize a history write.

- `commit`, `commit --amend`, `push`, `tag`, `rebase`, `cherry-pick`, `revert`,
  `merge`, branch deletion, `reset --hard`, path restore, and `clean -f` all
  require an explicit ask.
- Never publish merely because publication would be useful.

## Before an authorized discard

Recovery is insurance, not authorization. A save never expands what the user
allowed you to delete or overwrite.

When the user explicitly authorized an operation that may discard or broadly
overwrite workspace changes, and the workspace is an ordinary Git checkout:

1. After `muse.read_skill` gives the physical Git skill package path, run:

   ```bash
   bash <git-skill-dir>/scripts/workspace-recovery.sh save before-discard
   ```

2. Keep the printed `refs/tbh/recovery/...` value in your handoff, then perform
   only the exact authorized operation.
3. If the save fails or the workspace is unsupported, stop before destruction
   and ask the user.

To recover that saved tree later, run:

```bash
bash <git-skill-dir>/scripts/workspace-recovery.sh restore <recovery-ref>
```

Restore first saves the current workspace, leaves HEAD, branch, and the real
index in place, and restores the selected snapshot into the worktree. The ref
also retains distinct staged bytes when the same path had later worktree edits.
Read those staged bytes with `git show '<recovery-ref>^2:<path>'`; the recovery
commit's second parent is the saved index tree. Ignored files are not saved;
restore refuses an ignored-path collision rather than overwrite data it could
not save. Use only the exact printed ref, not a revision expression.

## Always fine

Read-only inspection such as `status`, `log`, `show`, `diff`, `blame`,
`branch -v`, `show-ref`, `rev-parse`, `for-each-ref`, and `merge-base` is fine.
Staging named files to inspect `diff --cached`, and a temporary stash around a
tool that requires a clean tree, are also fine when the original state is put
back afterward.

## The rest

- Do not use a broad add in a tree you did not clean; name the files you changed.
- Do not initialize a repository inside vendored, build, data, or existing
  source-control trees.
- Do not create or edit `.gitignore` or `.git/info/exclude` to hide the user's
  files, and do not stash the user's files (including `stash push -u`) to make
  `git status` look clean. "Leave the working tree clean", "tidy up", and
  similar phrasing do not authorize committing, pushing, ignoring, excluding,
  stashing, or deleting the user's files; clean up only scratch you created
  and say the user's files remain.
- Do not hand-edit generated files; change their source of truth.
- Scratch repositories under a temporary directory are yours to experiment in.

## Locks and corrupt state

A Git lock usually means another process is writing. Never kill the holder on
your own initiative. Wait, inspect the holder read-only, use that tool's normal
stop mechanism, or report the block. Never delete a lock without proving no
live process owns it, and never respond to index corruption by deleting state
and committing anyway.

Never commit or push while status reports changes you did not make and cannot
explain.

## If you already made an unwanted write

Say so plainly and stop. Do not attempt more history surgery without direction.

</read-skill-result>
